claim: Recent studies suggested an essential role for seryl-tRNA synthetase (SerRS) in vascular development.
source: Recent studies suggested an essential role for seryl-tRNA synthetase (SerRS) in vascular development.
evidence: This is a summary statement in the abstract that references prior work, though specific citations are not included in this sentence.

claim: The role of SerRS in vascular development is specific to SerRS among all tRNA synthetases.
source: This role is specific to SerRS among all tRNA synthetases and is independent of its well-known aminoacylation function in protein synthesis.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract.

claim: The role of SerRS in vascular development is independent of its aminoacylation function in protein synthesis.
source: This role is specific to SerRS among all tRNA synthetases and is independent of its well-known aminoacylation function in protein synthesis.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract and is supported by prior studies mentioned in the introduction.

claim: A unique nucleus-directing domain, added at the invertebrate-to-vertebrate transition, confers the novel non-translational activity of SerRS.
source: A unique nucleus-directing domain, added at the invertebrate-to-vertebrate transition, confers this novel non-translational activity of SerRS.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract, drawing on evolutionary and structural knowledge.

claim: Previous studies showed that SerRS controls VEGFA expression to prevent vascular over-expansion.
source: Previous studies showed that SerRS, in some unknown way, controls VEGFA expression to prevent vascular over-expansion.
evidence: This references prior work as background knowledge.

claim: SerRS antagonizes c-Myc, the major transcription factor promoting VEGFA expression.
source: Using in vitro, cell and animal experiments, we show here that SerRS intervenes by antagonizing c-Myc, the major transcription factor promoting VEGFA expression, through a tandem mechanism.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by multiple experimental approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: Nuclear-localized SerRS blocks c-Myc from binding to the VEGFA promoter by direct head-to-head competition.
source: First, by direct head-to-head competition, nuclear-localized SerRS blocks c-Myc from binding to the VEGFA promoter.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including ChIP and EMSA assays.

claim: DNA-bound SerRS recruits the SIRT2 histone deacetylase to erase prior c-Myc-promoted histone acetylation.
source: Second, DNA-bound SerRS recruits the SIRT2 histone deacetylase to erase prior c-Myc-promoted histone acetylation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including co-immunoprecipitation and ChIP assays.

claim: Vertebrate SerRS and c-Myc is a pair of 'Yin-Yang' transcriptional regulator for proper development of a functional vasculature.
source: Thus, vertebrate SerRS and c-Myc is a pair of 'Yin-Yang' transcriptional regulator for proper development of a functional vasculature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: SIRT2 has an anti-angiogenic activity.
source: Our results also discover an anti-angiogenic activity for SIRT2.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by zebrafish experiments showing that SIRT2 knockdown causes vascular over-expansion.

claim: Three independent forward genetics studies in zebrafish suggested an essential role for SerRS in vascular development.
source: Surprisingly, three independent forward genetics studies in zebrafish suggested an essential role for seryl-tRNA synthetase (SerRS) in vascular development (Amsterdam et al., 2004; Fukui et al., 2009; Herzog et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by three cited references.

claim: Disruption of sars in fish embryos through insertional mutagenesis caused excessive and abnormal blood vessel growth.
source: In fish embryos, disruption of sars (gene encoding SerRS), through insertional mutagenesis (Amsterdam et al., 2004) or ENU mutagenesis-induced point/truncation mutations (Fukui et al., 2009; Herzog et al., 2009), caused excessive and abnormal blood vessel growth.
evidence: This is supported by cited references to prior studies.

claim: The role of SerRS in vascular development is independent of its enzymatic activity.
source: However, the role of SerRS in vascular development is independent of its enzymatic activity (Fukui et al., 2009), but dependent on its vertebrate-specific, non-catalytic, C-terminal domain UNE-S (Guo et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2012; Guo and Schimmel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: The role of SerRS in vascular development is dependent on its vertebrate-specific, non-catalytic, C-terminal domain UNE-S.
source: However, the role of SerRS in vascular development is independent of its enzymatic activity (Fukui et al., 2009), but dependent on its vertebrate-specific, non-catalytic, C-terminal domain UNE-S (Guo et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2012; Guo and Schimmel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: The UNE-S domain contains a robust nuclear localization signal (NLS) sequence that directs a substantial amount of cellular SerRS into the nucleus in human cells.
source: The UNE-S domain contains a robust nuclear localization signal (NLS) sequence that, at least in human cells, directs a substantial amount of cellular SerRS into the nucleus (Guo et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2012; Guo and Schimmel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited references.

claim: All non-null mutations of sars linked to vasculature abnormalities either have the NLS truncated or conformationally sequestered, rendering deficient SerRS nuclear localization.
source: Remarkably, all non-null mutations of sars linked to vasculature abnormalities in the aforementioned genetics studies either have the NLS truncated or conformationally sequestered, and thus render deficient SerRS nuclear localization (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Zebrafish expressing engineered catalytically active but NLS-mutated SerRS exhibited the same abnormal blood vessel phenotype as observed in the sars mutant embryos.
source: Conversely, zebrafish expressing engineered catalytically active but NLS-mutated SerRS exhibited the same abnormal blood vessel phenotype as observed in the sars mutant embryos (Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: The essential role of SerRS in vascular development arises from its evolutionarily acquired nuclear presence.
source: Therefore, it has been clearly established that the essential role of SerRS in vascular development arises from its evolutionarily acquired nuclear presence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from cited prior work.

claim: Vascular abnormalities associated with deficient SerRS nuclear localization were accompanied with a high level of vegfa transcript in mutant fish embryos.
source: Interestingly, the vascular abnormalities associated with deficient SerRS nuclear localization were found to be accompanied with a high level of vegfa (Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor A) transcript in the mutant fish embryos (Fukui et al., 2009; Xu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: The nuclear function of SerRS in zebrafish is linked to attenuating the expression of Vegfa.
source: This observation suggested that the nuclear function of SerRS in zebrafish is linked to attenuating the expression of Vegfa.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from prior observations.

claim: VEGFA is a key stimulator of vasculogenesis and angiogenesis for all vertebrates.
source: Because VEGFA is a key stimulator of vasculogenesis and angiogenesis for all vertebrates, and over-expression of VEGFA is not only associated with developmental vascular abnormalities, but also contributes to various diseases including cancer (Drake and Little, 1995), we were motivated to determine whether the VEGFA-regulating function of SerRS is conserved in higher vertebrates such as humans, and what is the mechanism by which nuclear SerRS controls VEGFA expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Over-expression of VEGFA is associated with developmental vascular abnormalities and contributes to various diseases including cancer.
source: Because VEGFA is a key stimulator of vasculogenesis and angiogenesis for all vertebrates, and over-expression of VEGFA is not only associated with developmental vascular abnormalities, but also contributes to various diseases including cancer (Drake and Little, 1995), we were motivated to determine whether the VEGFA-regulating function of SerRS is conserved in higher vertebrates such as humans, and what is the mechanism by which nuclear SerRS controls VEGFA expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: c-Myc is the major transcription factor promoting VEGFA gene expression in the nucleus.
source: It is well established that c-Myc is the major transcription factor promoting VEGFA gene expression in the nucleus, and thereby has a key role in vascular development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: c-Myc has a key role in vascular development.
source: It is well established that c-Myc is the major transcription factor promoting VEGFA gene expression in the nucleus, and thereby has a key role in vascular development.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: c-Myc functions through heterodimerization with MAX for binding to the E-box DNA sequence on its target genes.
source: As a basic helix-loop-helix-leucine zipper (bHLHZ) protein, c-Myc functions through heterodimerization with the small bHLHZ partner MAX for binding to the Enhancer Box (E-box) DNA sequence (5′-CACGTG-3′) on its target genes (Blackwood and Eisenman, 1991).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: DNA-bound c-Myc recruits histone acetyltransferase to acetylate histone proteins to allow chromatin expansion and activate transcription.
source: DNA-bound c-Myc recruits histone acetyltransferase to acetylate histone proteins to allow chromatin expansion and activate transcription (Grandori et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: c-Myc knockout mice are embryonic lethal and exhibit under-developed vasculature.
source: c-Myc knockout mice are embryonic lethal and exhibit, among others deformities, under-developed vasculature.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: Deformities in c-Myc knockout mice can be partially rescued by transgenic VEGFA expression.
source: Importantly, these deformities can be partially rescued by transgenic VEGFA expression (Baudino et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Endothelial-specific c-Myc overexpression in mice causes embryonic lethality arising from widespread edema, multiple hemorrhagic lesions and severe defects in the vascular network, accompanied by an elevated level of VEGFA.
source: On the other hand, endothelial-specific c-Myc overexpression in mice also causes embryonic lethality arising from widespread edema, multiple hemorrhagic lesions and severe defects in the vascular network, accompanied by an elevated level of VEGFA (Kokai et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: The role of c-Myc in vascular development and in promoting VEGFA expression has to be tightly balanced.
source: Together, these results suggest that the role of c-Myc in vascular development and in promoting VEGFA expression has to be tightly balanced.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited prior work.

claim: SerRS and c-Myc compete head-to-head for the same VEGFA promoter binding site.
source: We show a head-to-head competition between SerRS and c-Myc for the same VEGFA promoter binding site and, in addition, a direct recruitment of SIRT2 histone deacetylase by SerRS to erase the transcription-enhancing chromatin remodeling already instigated by c-Myc.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: SerRS directly recruits SIRT2 histone deacetylase to erase the transcription-enhancing chromatin remodeling instigated by c-Myc.
source: We show a head-to-head competition between SerRS and c-Myc for the same VEGFA promoter binding site and, in addition, a direct recruitment of SIRT2 histone deacetylase by SerRS to erase the transcription-enhancing chromatin remodeling already instigated by c-Myc.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: SerRS is a key balancing antagonist of c-Myc for regulation of VEGFA expression.
source: These results and further experiments in a vertebrate model organism reveal that SerRS is a key balancing antagonist of c-Myc for regulation of VEGFA expression, as well as for proper development of a functional vasculature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: SerRS is a key balancing antagonist of c-Myc for proper development of a functional vasculature.
source: These results and further experiments in a vertebrate model organism reveal that SerRS is a key balancing antagonist of c-Myc for regulation of VEGFA expression, as well as for proper development of a functional vasculature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: SIRT2 has an anti-angiogenic function that arises at least in part through its interaction with SerRS.
source: In addition, our study provides the first report of an anti-angiogenic function for SIRT2, which arises at least in part through its interaction with SerRS.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The level of VEGFA transcript was more than doubled in HUVECs expressing shRNA against SerRS compared to control shRNA.
source: For both cell types, the level of VEGFA transcript was more than doubled in cells expressing the shRNA against SerRS (sh-SerRS) vs a control shRNA (sh-Con) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cells expressing NLS-deleted SerRS resulted in three-fold higher expression of VEGFA in HUVECs compared to WT SerRS-expressing cells.
source: Remarkably, compared to WT SerRS-expressing cells, cells expressing ΔNLS SerRS resulted in three and fourfold higher expression of VEGFA in HUVECs (Figure 1A) and HEK293 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cells expressing NLS-deleted SerRS resulted in four-fold higher expression of VEGFA in HEK293 cells compared to WT SerRS-expressing cells.
source: Remarkably, compared to WT SerRS-expressing cells, cells expressing ΔNLS SerRS resulted in three and fourfold higher expression of VEGFA in HUVECs (Figure 1A) and HEK293 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The role of nuclear SerRS in suppressing VEGFA expression is conserved from fish to humans.
source: This result supports the idea that the role of nuclear SerRS in suppressing VEGFA expression is conserved from fish to humans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data comparing WT and NLS-deleted SerRS.

claim: HUVECs expressing NLS-deleted SerRS showed a much stronger propensity to form a blood vessel-like tubular network than WT SerRS-expressing cells.
source: In addition, as measured in an in vitro endothelial tube formation assay, and consistent with the role of VEGFA in promoting angiogenesis, HUVECs expressing ΔNLS SerRS showed a much stronger propensity (than WT SerRS-expressing cells) to form a blood vessel-like tubular network (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Purified SerRS bound to DNA, but two other human tRNA synthetases (GlyRS and LysRS) did not.
source: Using cellulose beads-linked calf thymus DNA, we found that purified SerRS, but not two other human tRNA synthetases (GlyRS and LysRS), bound to DNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ectopically expressed SerRS bound to the VEGFA promoter in the region from −1.5 kb to +1 of the transcription start site.
source: We found that ectopically expressed SerRS bound to the promoter in the region from −1.5 kb to +1 of the start site.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The SerRS binding region on the VEGFA promoter encompasses the binding site of c-Myc.
source: Importantly, this region encompasses the binding site of c-Myc on the VEGFA promoter (Figure 2B; Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data and a cited reference.

claim: SerRS overexpression sharply reduced the elicitation of luciferase activity driven by the VEGFA promoter.
source: Strikingly, SerRS overexpression sharply reduced the elicitation of luciferase activity (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Overexpression of GlyRS had no effect on luciferase activity driven by the VEGFA promoter.
source: In contrast, overexpression of GlyRS, which lacks DNA-binding capacity, had no effect (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The SerRS-specific responsive element on the VEGFA promoter is within the 308-bp region from −262 to +46.
source: In further work, we showed that the inhibitory effect of SerRS persisted as the promoter region was shortened to −262 ∼ +46, suggesting that the SerRS-specific responsive element is within this 308-bp region (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Purified SerRS protected a 25-bp region (−62 to −38) on the VEGFA promoter from DNase I digestion in a concentration dependent manner.
source: As shown in Figure 2D, purified SerRS protected a 25-bp region (−62 ∼ −38) from DNase I digestion and did so in a concentration dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The binding affinity (Kd) of SerRS to the 27-bp DNA fragment from the VEGFA promoter was 211.5 nM as measured by EMSA.
source: The binding affinity (Kd) of SerRS was 211.5 nM as measured by EMSA (Figure 3A,B) and 265 nM by surface plasmon resonance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The binding affinity (Kd) of SerRS to the 27-bp DNA fragment from the VEGFA promoter was 265 nM as measured by surface plasmon resonance.
source: The binding affinity (Kd) of SerRS was 211.5 nM as measured by EMSA (Figure 3A,B) and 265 nM by surface plasmon resonance (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The DNA minimal binding site of SerRS on the VEGFA promoter was determined to be 21 nt (−59 to −38).
source: Interestingly, truncations from both ends of the 27-bp DNA fragment weakened the interaction and, based on the EMSA analysis, the DNA minimal binding site of SerRS was determined to be 21 nt (−59 ∼ −38) (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The c-Myc/MAX binding site on the VEGFA promoter is from −53 to −38 and contains a nonclassical E-box sequence (−49CATGCG−44).
source: The c-Myc/MAX binding site (−53 ∼ −38) contains a nonclassical E-box sequence (−49CATGCG−44) that completely overlaps with the SerRS binding site (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The c-Myc/MAX binding site completely overlaps with the SerRS binding site on the VEGFA promoter.
source: The c-Myc/MAX binding site (−53 ∼ −38) contains a nonclassical E-box sequence (−49CATGCG−44) that completely overlaps with the SerRS binding site (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Two double mutants of the E-box sequence did not affect SerRS interaction with DNA.
source: Two double mutants of the E-box, including one (−49CTTACG−44) that would completely abolish c-Myc/Max binding (Blackwell et al., 1993), did not affect the SerRS interaction (Figure 4A)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Five different single mutations outside the E-box greatly weakened SerRS binding to DNA.
source: on the other hand, five different single mutations outside the E-box (on both the 5′ and the 3′ sides) that would not affect c-Myc/Max binding greatly weakened SerRS binding (Figure 4A), indicating that SerRS and c-Myc/Max have distinct DNA binding specificities.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SerRS and c-Myc/Max have distinct DNA binding specificities.
source: on the other hand, five different single mutations outside the E-box (on both the 5′ and the 3′ sides) that would not affect c-Myc/Max binding greatly weakened SerRS binding (Figure 4A), indicating that SerRS and c-Myc/Max have distinct DNA binding specificities.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mutagenesis data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of TBD or UNE-S dramatically weakens or completely abolishes the DNA interaction of SerRS.
source: Deletion of TBD or UNE-S dramatically weakens or completely abolishes the DNA interaction (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only the intact SerRS can bind to DNA.
source: In fact, only the intact SerRS can bind to DNA (Figure 4B), suggesting that multiple domains of SerRS contribute to the DNA interaction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Multiple domains of SerRS contribute to the DNA interaction.
source: In fact, only the intact SerRS can bind to DNA (Figure 4B), suggesting that multiple domains of SerRS contribute to the DNA interaction.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the domain deletion data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Deletion of each of the two higher eukaryote-specific insertions in TBD and CD dramatically weakens the DNA interaction of SerRS.
source: Deletion of each of the two higher eukaryote-specific insertions in TBD and CD, respectively, which does not negatively impact tRNA binding (Xu et al., 2013), dramatically weakens the DNA interaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Deletion of ΔV2-G14 in TBD abolishes the DNA binding of SerRS.
source: Two additional deletions—ΔV2-G14 in TBD and ΔT413-V420 in CD—also abolish the DNA binding (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Deletion of ΔT413-V420 in CD abolishes the DNA binding of SerRS.
source: Two additional deletions—ΔV2-G14 in TBD and ΔT413-V420 in CD—also abolish the DNA binding (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The binding affinity of the c-Myc/MAX–DNA interaction is 90.5 to 229 nM.
source: It is important to note that the binding affinity of the SerRS–DNA interaction (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) is comparable to that of the c-Myc/MAX–DNA interaction (90.5 ∼ 229 nM) (Hu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Ectopic expression of WT SerRS repressed the overexpression of VEGFA driven by c-Myc in HEK 293 cells.
source: Indeed, in HEK 293 cells and measuring by real time qRT-PCR, ectopic expression of WT (but not NLS-deleted) SerRS repressed the overexpression of VEGFA driven by c-Myc (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ectopic expression of NLS-deleted SerRS did not repress the overexpression of VEGFA driven by c-Myc in HEK 293 cells.
source: Indeed, in HEK 293 cells and measuring by real time qRT-PCR, ectopic expression of WT (but not NLS-deleted) SerRS repressed the overexpression of VEGFA driven by c-Myc (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SerRS can compete in vitro with the c-Myc/MAX complex for binding to the 27-bp DNA fragment from the VEGFA promoter at the same concentrations.
source: Consistently, our EMSA and Western blot analyses clearly showed that SerRS, at the same concentrations, could compete in vitro with the c-Myc/MAX complex for binding to the 27-bp DNA fragment from the VEGFA promoter (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SerRS cannot compete with the MAX/MAX homodimer for binding to the DNA at comparable concentrations.
source: We note that SerRS cannot compete with the MAX/MAX homodimer for binding to the DNA at comparable concentrations (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), presumably because of the tight DNA binding affinity of the MAX/MAX homodimer (19.2 ∼ 48.7 nM) (Hu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The tight DNA binding affinity of the MAX/MAX homodimer is 19.2 to 48.7 nM.
source: We note that SerRS cannot compete with the MAX/MAX homodimer for binding to the DNA at comparable concentrations (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), presumably because of the tight DNA binding affinity of the MAX/MAX homodimer (19.2 ∼ 48.7 nM) (Hu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Ectopically expressed WT SerRS could compete c-Myc off of the VEGFA promoter in HEK 293 cells.
source: ChIP analysis showed that ectopically expressed WT, but not NLS-deleted, SerRS could compete c-Myc off of the VEGFA promoter in HEK 293 cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ectopically expressed NLS-deleted SerRS could not compete c-Myc off of the VEGFA promoter in HEK 293 cells.
source: ChIP analysis showed that ectopically expressed WT, but not NLS-deleted, SerRS could compete c-Myc off of the VEGFA promoter in HEK 293 cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Knocking down endogenous SerRS expression in HUVEC cells resulted in a dramatic increase of endogenous c-Myc binding to the VEGFA promoter.
source: Consistently, knocking down endogenous SerRS expression in HUVEC cells resulted in a dramatic increase of endogenous c-Myc binding to the VEGFA promoter (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The increase in c-Myc binding to the VEGFA promoter caused by SerRS knockdown was completely reversed when cells were compensated with ectopically expressed WT SerRS.
source: This increase was completely reversed when the cells were compensated with ectopically expressed WT, but not NLS-deleted, SerRS (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The increase in c-Myc binding to the VEGFA promoter caused by SerRS knockdown was not reversed when cells were compensated with ectopically expressed NLS-deleted SerRS.
source: This increase was completely reversed when the cells were compensated with ectopically expressed WT, but not NLS-deleted, SerRS (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SerRS is a potent endogenous inhibitor of c-Myc for binding to the VEGFA promoter.
source: These results suggest that SerRS is a potent endogenous inhibitor of c-Myc for binding to the VEGFA promoter, and vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the ChIP data in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Knocking down SerRS by injection of an antisense morpholino resulted in a hyper-intersegmental vessel (ISV) branching phenotype in zebrafish.
source: As expected (Fukui et al., 2009), knocking down SerRS by injection of an antisense morpholino (SerRS-MO) resulted in a hyper-intersegmental vessel (ISV) branching phenotype in zebrafish (Figure 5E), and the phenotype was accompanied with an elevated level of Vefga expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The hyper-ISV phenotype caused by SerRS knockdown in zebrafish was accompanied with an elevated level of Vegfa expression.
source: As expected (Fukui et al., 2009), knocking down SerRS by injection of an antisense morpholino (SerRS-MO) resulted in a hyper-intersegmental vessel (ISV) branching phenotype in zebrafish (Figure 5E), and the phenotype was accompanied with an elevated level of Vefga expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Out of 130 fish embryos injected with SerRS-MO, 72 (55.4%) exhibited hyper-ISV phenotype.
source: Specifically, out of 130 fish embryos injected with SerRS-MO, 72 (55.4%) exhibited hyper-ISV phenotype, as oppose to 2.9% (n = 4 out of 140) of fish injected with a control morpholino (control-MO).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: 2.9% (n = 4 out of 140) of fish injected with control morpholino exhibited hyper-ISV phenotype.
source: Specifically, out of 130 fish embryos injected with SerRS-MO, 72 (55.4%) exhibited hyper-ISV phenotype, as oppose to 2.9% (n = 4 out of 140) of fish injected with a control morpholino (control-MO).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Knocking down c-Myc by injecting an antisense morpholino against Myca showed under-developed vasculature in zebrafish.
source: In contrast, knocking down c-Myc by injecting an antisense morpholino against Myca (c-Myc homologue in zebrafish) showed under-developed vasculature, which is accompanied with a reduced level of Vefga expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Knocking down c-Myc in zebrafish is accompanied with a reduced level of Vegfa expression.
source: In contrast, knocking down c-Myc by injecting an antisense morpholino against Myca (c-Myc homologue in zebrafish) showed under-developed vasculature, which is accompanied with a reduced level of Vefga expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: 41.4% (n = 24 out of 58) of Myca-MO-injected morphants exhibits hypo-ISV phenotype.
source: In particular, 41.4% (n = 24 out of 58) of Myca-MO-injected morphants exhibits hypo-ISV phenotype, as opposed to 10% (n = 14 out of 140) of control-MO-injected morphants (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: 10% (n = 14 out of 140) of control-MO-injected morphants exhibits hypo-ISV phenotype.
source: In particular, 41.4% (n = 24 out of 58) of Myca-MO-injected morphants exhibits hypo-ISV phenotype, as opposed to 10% (n = 14 out of 140) of control-MO-injected morphants (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Co-injection of Myca-MO with SerRS-MO efficiently rescued both hyper-ISV (10.7%, n = 18 out of 169) and hypo-ISV (10.1%, n = 17 out of 169) defects in zebrafish.
source: Remarkably, co-injection of Myca-MO with SerRS-MO efficiently rescued both hyper-ISV (10.7%, n = 18 out of 169) and hypo-ISV (10.1%, n = 17 out of 169) defects (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Co-injection of Myca-MO partially reversed the high Vegfa expression level in SerRS-MO-injected zebrafish.
source: Coincidently, co-injection of Myca-MO also partially reversed the high Vegfa expression level in SerRS-MO-injected zebrafish (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A counteracting effect between c-Myc and SerRS in vascular development was confirmed in a vertebrate system.
source: Therefore, a counteracting effect between c-Myc and SerRS in vascular development was confirmed in a vertebrate system.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the zebrafish rescue experiments.

claim: A delicate balance between SerRS and c-Myc is essential for developing a functional vasculature.
source: These results highlight a 'Yin-Yang' regulation of SerRS and c-Myc on VEGFA expression and demonstrate that a delicate balance between them is essential for developing a functional vasculature.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the zebrafish experiments.

claim: A large scale protein–protein interaction study indicated a potential interaction between SerRS and sirtuin 2 (SIRT2).
source: A large scale protein–protein interaction study indicated a potential interaction between SerRS and sirtuin 2 (SIRT2) (Ewing et al., 2007), a NAD+-dependent histone deacetylase of the sirtuin family that regulates a broad range of processes, including transcription, metabolism, neurodegeneration, and aging (Finkel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: SIRT2 is a NAD+-dependent histone deacetylase of the sirtuin family that regulates transcription, metabolism, neurodegeneration, and aging.
source: A large scale protein–protein interaction study indicated a potential interaction between SerRS and sirtuin 2 (SIRT2) (Ewing et al., 2007), a NAD+-dependent histone deacetylase of the sirtuin family that regulates a broad range of processes, including transcription, metabolism, neurodegeneration, and aging (Finkel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: c-Myc activates gene expression by recruiting partners harboring histone acetyltransferase activity that modifies histones and leads to open chromatin structures.
source: Considering that c-Myc activates gene expression by recruiting partners harboring histone acetyltransferase activity that modifies histones and leads to open chromatin structures (McMahon et al., 1998, 2000; Amati et al., 2001), we postulated that an interaction between SerRS and SIRT2 might reverse this process to attenuate VEGFA expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Ectopically expressed SIRT2, but not SIRT1, effectively pulled down SerRS.
source: The ectopically expressed SIRT2, but not SIRT1, effectively pulled down SerRS, and vice versa (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The interaction between endogenous SerRS and SIRT2 was confirmed by coimmunoprecipitation.
source: The interaction between endogenous SerRS and SIRT2 was also confirmed by coimmunoprecipitation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A purified GST-SerRS fusion protein successfully pulled down purified SIRT2, showing that the protein–protein interaction is direct.
source: Moreover, a purified GST-SerRS fusion protein successfully pulled down purified SIRT2, thus showing that the protein–protein interaction is direct (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The catalytic domain (CD) of SerRS is responsible for the interaction with SIRT2.
source: Further mapping analysis showed that the catalytic domain (CD) of SerRS is responsible for the interaction with SIRT2 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of SerRS, but not GlyRS, significantly reduced the amount of SIRT2 bound to the VEGFA promoter.
source: Knockdown of SerRS, but not GlyRS, significantly reduced the amount to SIRT2 bound to the VEGFA promoter (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), demonstrating that SerRS specifically recruits SIRT2 to the VEGFA promoter.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: SerRS specifically recruits SIRT2 to the VEGFA promoter.
source: Knockdown of SerRS, but not GlyRS, significantly reduced the amount to SIRT2 bound to the VEGFA promoter (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), demonstrating that SerRS specifically recruits SIRT2 to the VEGFA promoter.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Residues within the regions of G52-D60 and W337-S356 of SIRT2 are critical for interaction with SerRS.
source: Particularly, residues within the regions of G52-D60 and W337-S356 are critical, as the loss of either region abolished the interaction of SIRT2 with SerRS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both SerRS binding regions on SIRT2 are located on the opposite side of the substrate-binding pocket.
source: Interestingly, both regions are located on the opposite side of the substrate-binding pocket (Figure 6D), suggesting that bound SerRS should not interfere with the deacetylase activity of SIRT2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from structural analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: At an equal molar ratio (1:1), SerRS did not inhibit but rather promoted the deacetylase activity of SIRT2.
source: Remarkably, at an equal molar ratio (1:1), SerRS did not inhibit but rather promoted the deacetylase activity of SIRT2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The evolutionally conserved deacetylase activity of SIRT2 has a strong preference for K16 of histone H4.
source: Because the evolutionally conserved deacetylase activity of SIRT2 has a strong preference for K16 of histone H4 (Vaquero et al., 2006), we performed ChIP analyses using antibodies against acetylated H4K16 (H4K16Ac).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Overexpression of SerRS, but not of GlyRS, reduced the level of H4K16Ac on the VEGFA promoter.
source: Remarkably, overexpression of SerRS, but not of GlyRS, reduced the level of H4K16Ac on the VEGFA promoter (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Knocking down endogenous SerRS, but not endogenous GlyRS, significantly increased H4K16Ac on the VEGFA promoter.
source: Consistently, knocking down endogenous SerRS, but not endogenous GlyRS, had the opposite effect and significantly increased H4K16Ac on the VEGFA promoter (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The increase in H4K16Ac caused by SerRS knockdown was reversed when cells were compensated with WT, but not NLS-deleted, SerRS.
source: The increase was reversed when the cells were compensated with WT, but not NLS-deleted, SerRS (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Nuclear SerRS acts to decrease the amount of acetylated H4 on the VEGFA promoter.
source: These results demonstrated that nuclear SerRS acts to decrease the amount of acetylated H4 on the VEGFA promoter.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ChIP data in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Knocking down the expression of SIRT2, but not of SIRT1, completely reversed the transcriptional repression activity of SerRS on VEGFA expression.
source: Indeed, knocking down the expression of SIRT2, but not of SIRT1, completely reversed the transcriptional repression activity of SerRS on VEGFA expression (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Inhibiting SIRT2 activity by AGK2 completely knocked out the transcriptional repression activity of SerRS.
source: Consistently, inhibiting SIRT2 activity by AGK2, a SIRT2-specific inhibitor (Outeiro et al., 2007), also completely knocked out the transcriptional repression activity of SerRS, while EX-527, a SIRT1 inhibitor (Solomon et al., 2006), had little effect (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: EX-527, a SIRT1 inhibitor, had little effect on the transcriptional repression activity of SerRS.
source: Consistently, inhibiting SIRT2 activity by AGK2, a SIRT2-specific inhibitor (Outeiro et al., 2007), also completely knocked out the transcriptional repression activity of SerRS, while EX-527, a SIRT1 inhibitor (Solomon et al., 2006), had little effect (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: SIRT1 has been shown to promote angiogenesis.
source: While SIRT1 has been shown to promote angiogenesis (Potente et al., 2007), the role of SIRT2 in vascular development has not been clear.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Injection of an antisense morpholino against Sirt1 generated the hypo-ISV phenotype in zebrafish.
source: Consistent with the previous report showing a VEGFA-independent pro-angiogenic role for SIRT1 in vascular development (Potente et al., 2007), injection of an antisense morpholino against Sirt1 (SIRT1 homologue in zebrafish) generated the hypo-ISV phenotype (Figure 7E) and had no significant effect on Vegfa expression (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E and 7F.

claim: Injection of Sirt1-MO had no significant effect on Vegfa expression in zebrafish.
source: Consistent with the previous report showing a VEGFA-independent pro-angiogenic role for SIRT1 in vascular development (Potente et al., 2007), injection of an antisense morpholino against Sirt1 (SIRT1 homologue in zebrafish) generated the hypo-ISV phenotype (Figure 7E) and had no significant effect on Vegfa expression (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Injection of Sirt2-MO resulted in the same hyper-ISV phenotype (42.1%, n = 75 out 178) as with the injection of SerRS-MO (46.7%, n = 119 out of 255).
source: In contrast, injection of a Sirt2-MO resulted in the same hyper-ISV phenotype (42.1%, n = 75 out 178) as with the injection of SerRS-MO (46.7%, n = 119 out of 255) (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The hyper-ISV phenotype caused by Sirt2-MO and SerRS-MO was accompanied by a significantly elevated level of the vegfa transcript.
source: Furthermore, the hyper-ISV phenotype, in both cases, was accompanied by a significantly elevated level of the vegfa transcript (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: SIRT2 has an anti-angiogenic role that is at least in part dependent on attenuating VEGFA expression through its interaction with SerRS.
source: Therefore, our studies have revealed an anti-angiogenic role of SIRT2, which should be, at least in part, dependent on attenuating VEGFA expression through its interaction with SerRS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the zebrafish experiments.

claim: The essential role of SerRS in vascular development arises from its novel activities as a transcriptional repressor of VEGFA.
source: Through in vitro, cell-based and animal experiments, we established that the essential role of SerRS in vascular development arises from its novel activities as a transcriptional repressor of VEGFA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Mad family proteins are generally considered as antagonists of c-Myc with regard to the role of c-Myc in tumorigenesis.
source: Therefore, Mad proteins are generally considered as antagonists of c-Myc, especially with regard to the role of c-Myc in tumorigenesis (Zhou and Hurlin, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Disruption of members of the Mad family in mice does not exhibit any vascular phenotype.
source: However, the role of Mad proteins in vascular development appears to be non-essential. Disruption of members of the Mad family in mice does not exhibit any vascular phenotype (Foley et al., 1998; Schreiber-Agus et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by cited references.

claim: c-Myc is expressed during development, while expression of Mad proteins is mainly induced during terminal differentiation.
source: In addition, the temporal expression pattern varies between c-Myc and the Mad family proteins, with c-Myc being expressed during development, while expression of Mad proteins is mainly induced during terminal differentiation (Queva et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a cited reference.

claim: Mad proteins are largely silent during the time that the vasculature is being established.
source: Thus, the Mad proteins are largely silent during the time that the vasculature is being established, which could explain their non-essential role in vascular development.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal expression pattern of Mad proteins.

claim: A closed circulatory system with vasculature network is one of the hallmarks of vertebrates.
source: From an evolutionary perspective, a closed circulatory system with vasculature network is one of the hallmarks of vertebrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: The c-Myc gene first appeared in Drosophila, an invertebrate with a primitive 'open' circulatory system.
source: Although c-Myc plays a key role in vascular development, the gene first appeared in Drosphila, an invertebrate with a primitive 'open' circulatory system.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: The MAX and Mad family genes first appeared in roundworms such as C. elegans.
source: The appearance of the MAX and Mad family genes is even earlier, and the genes were first identified in roundworms such as C. elegans (Atchley and Fitch, 1995; Prendergast, 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The UNE-S domain of SerRS only appeared in vertebrates.
source: In contrast, although SerRS is considered as one of the most ancient proteins, its UNE-S domain, which harbors the NLS signal to endow SerRS with its novel transcription repressor activity, only appeared in vertebrates.
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: An 'old' tRNA synthetase evolved to function as a 'new' and essential antagonist against c-Myc for proper development of the advanced closed circulatory system of vertebrates.
source: Thus, it seems that an 'old' tRNA synthetase evolved to function as a 'new' and essential antagonist against c-Myc for proper development of the advanced closed circulatory system of vertebrates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from evolutionary considerations.

claim: A complete reversal of the inhibitory effect of SerRS on VEGFA expression was observed when SIRT2 was knocked out by RNAi or inhibited by EX527.
source: In fact, a complete reversal of the inhibitory effect of SerRS on VEGFA expression was observed when SIRT2 was knocked out by RNAi or inhibited by EX527 (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: The transcriptional repressor role of SerRS is ultimately through SIRT2.
source: This observation indicates that the transcriptional repressor role of SerRS is ultimately through SIRT2 and that the direct blocking of c-Myc from the promoter by SerRS may have lesser significance for downregulating gene expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the SIRT2 knockdown/inhibition experiments.

claim: The direct blocking of c-Myc from the promoter by SerRS may have lesser significance for downregulating gene expression.
source: This observation indicates that the transcriptional repressor role of SerRS is ultimately through SIRT2 and that the direct blocking of c-Myc from the promoter by SerRS may have lesser significance for downregulating gene expression.
evidence: This is speculation based on the SIRT2 knockdown/inhibition experiments.

claim: An overlapping DNA binding site may not be a prerequisite for SerRS to antagonize c-Myc, as long as both SerRS and c-Myc bind to the same promoter.
source: Thus, an overlapping DNA binding site may not be a prerequisite for SerRS to antagonize c-Myc, as long as both SerRS and c-Myc bind to the same promoter.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mechanism of SerRS action.

claim: Additional genes may be transcriptionally repressed by SerRS, presumably through its collaboration with SIRT2.
source: Considering the large number of genes that are regulated by c-Myc, one would not be surprised to find additional genes to be transcriptionally repressed by SerRS, presumably also through its collaboration with SIRT2.
evidence: This is speculation based on the mechanism of SerRS action.

claim: SIRT2 has been identified as a tumor suppressor.
source: It is worth noting that SIRT2 has been identified as a tumor suppressor (Hiratsuka et al., 2003; Lennerz et al., 2005), while c-Myc is a prominent oncogene that promotes tumor cell proliferation and tumor vascularization (Baudino et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: c-Myc is a prominent oncogene that promotes tumor cell proliferation and tumor vascularization.
source: It is worth noting that SIRT2 has been identified as a tumor suppressor (Hiratsuka et al., 2003; Lennerz et al., 2005), while c-Myc is a prominent oncogene that promotes tumor cell proliferation and tumor vascularization (Baudino et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: SerRS may function as a tumor suppressor by collaborating with SIRT2 to antagonize c-Myc.
source: We speculate that SerRS also functions as a tumor suppressor by collaborating with SIRT2 to antagonize c-Myc.
evidence: This is speculation based on the known roles of SIRT2 and c-Myc in cancer.

claim: Human SARS is located on the short arm of chromosome 1 (i.e., 1p13.3).
source: Interestingly, human SARS is located on the short arm of chromosome 1 (i.e., 1p13.3), which is frequently affected by rearrangements or allelic loss in a variety of human malignancies (Morgan et al., 1985; Mitchell and Santibanez-Koref, 1990; Mathew et al., 1994; Munn et al., 1995; Nagai et al., 1995; Xu et al., 2001; Caramazza et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Chromosome 1p13.3 is frequently affected by rearrangements or allelic loss in a variety of human malignancies.
source: Interestingly, human SARS is located on the short arm of chromosome 1 (i.e., 1p13.3), which is frequently affected by rearrangements or allelic loss in a variety of human malignancies (Morgan et al., 1985; Mitchell and Santibanez-Koref, 1990; Mathew et al., 1994; Munn et al., 1995; Nagai et al., 1995; Xu et al., 2001; Caramazza et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The frequent disruption of chromosome 1p13.3 in human malignancies suggests the presence of tumor suppressor genes which, when perturbed, lead to increased cancer susceptibility.
source: The frequent disruption of this chromosomal locus in human malignancies suggests the presence of tumor suppressor genes which, when perturbed, lead to increased cancer susceptibility.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the chromosomal location data.

claim: If SerRS is a factor in malignancies, its function in translation would need to be preserved, which could be achieved by disruption of the UNE-S domain.
source: Because SerRS is also essential for survival through its function in protein synthesis, if it is a factor in any of these malignancies, then its function in translation would need to be preserved. This could be achieved by disruption of the UNE-S domain, which does not affect aminoacylation, but is essential for SerRS to antagonize c-Myc.
evidence: This is speculation based on the dual functions of SerRS.
